chapter_theme: Kayasandigai tells Manimekalai why Aathirai's house should give the first alms: Aathirai's husband Saathuvan, ruined by a courtesan and dice, was wrecked at sea and reported dead; Aathirai entered a funeral fire that would not burn her, and a heavenly voice promised his return; on the island of the naked cannibal Nagas Saathuvan, knowing their language, refused their woman, liquor and meat, argued for rebirth from the corpse and the dream, gave their chief a dharma he could keep, and came home with treasure. Aathirai then fills the bowl Amudasurabi, praying that hunger leave the whole earth.

cast.role: a vidyadhara woman cursed with an insatiable hunger, who tells Manimekalai Aathirai's story
Madhavi's daughter, a Buddhist mendicant carrying the bowl Amudasurabi
a chaste wife of Puhar whom fire would not burn; she gives the first alms into the bowl
Aathirai's husband, a merchant ruined by a courtesan and dice, shipwrecked among the Nagas
the courtesan who kept Saathuvan and cast him off when his money was gone
the sea merchants Saathuvan sails with
the survivors of the wreck who report Saathuvan dead
the bodiless voice from the sky that tells Aathirai her husband lives
the naked Nagas of the island hill, eaters of shipwrecked men
the chief of the Nagas, called குருமகன், சிறுமகன் and எரி விழி நாகன்
the merchant whose ship brings Saathuvan home

manimekalai:16:1-21.reading: Kayasandigai begins Aathirai's story for Manimekalai: her husband Saathuvan, lacking worth, left her for a courtesan who fed him, squandered his wealth on dice and gaming, was cast off by the courtesan as a man without a coin once his wealth was gone, sailed off with merchants in restless desire, was wrecked, clung to a broken spar and was washed to the hill of the naked Nagas, while the men who escaped the wreck reported that he had died with the others in the dark sea.
manimekalai:16:1-21.nuance: The tale is told as a lesson attached to a house: Kayasandigai sends Manimekalai to Aathirai's door and then explains why it is the right first door, and she begins not with Aathirai's virtue but with her husband's fault (தகவு இலன், line 4). Line 16 tells the reader ahead of time that he came to belong to the Nagas (அவர் பான்மையன் ஆயினன்), so the survivors' report of his death at line 21 is known to be false before Aathirai hears it.
manimekalai:16:1-21.event: Saathuvan leaves Aathirai for a courtesan, loses his wealth at dice, is cast off, sails with merchants and is shipwrecked; survivors report him dead.

manimekalai:16:22-43.reading: Hearing the report, Aathirai calls on the townsfolk to give her a funeral pyre, digs a pit in the burning ground, lights a fire of dry wood and enters it saying she will go where her husband's deeds have carried him, but the fire touches neither her bed, her cloth, her sandal paste nor the garland in her hair, so that she sits in it unharmed like Lakshmi alone on a lotus, and when she cries that she is a woman of evil deeds whom even fire will not kill, a voice tells her that her husband reached the Naga hill and will come back on the ship of the merchant Chandradattan.
manimekalai:16:22-43.nuance: Aathirai reads the miracle backwards: the fire's refusal, which the story offers as proof of her virtue, she takes as proof of her own bad karma (தீயும் கொல்லாத் தீவினையாட்டியேன், line 35). Her reason for entering the fire is also karmic and not only grief: she means to follow her husband into whatever birth his deeds have led him (வினைப் பயன் உய்ப்ப, line 27). The lotus and the goddess on it (lines 33-34) echo the image by which Kayasandigai praised her at the close of the previous kaathai.
manimekalai:16:22-43.event: Aathirai enters a funeral fire for her husband; it does not burn her, and a voice from the sky tells her he lives and will return.

claims.claim: a wife may follow her dead husband into the place his deeds carry him
a woman whom even fire will not kill is held by her own evil deeds

manimekalai:16:44-59.reading: When the bodiless voice has spoken from the sky, Aathirai's tears cease, she goes home untroubled like a woman coming back from a bath in a pool and prays for her husband's quick return, becoming one whom even the chaste wives who never fail in merit and bring down the rain revere; meanwhile her husband, worn out by the sea, sleeps in a tree's shade on the shore of the high hill, and the unkind naked Nagas who live there find him and rouse him, saying that this lone, pitiable man come by himself is a body of flesh fit for food.
manimekalai:16:44-59.nuance: The rank given here goes beyond the rain-bringing wife: the women whose word brings rain themselves worship Aathirai (lines 49-51), so the test by fire sets her above the very standard of chastity. The simile at line 46, a woman returning from bathing in a pool, turns the pyre she has just left into water. The scene then cuts from a wife whose fire would not burn her body to a husband whose body is about to be eaten.
manimekalai:16:44-59.event: Aathirai goes home comforted; on the island the naked Nagas find the sleeping Saathuvan and mean to eat him.

claims.claim: chaste wives whose merit brings rain themselves worship the wife whom fire would not burn

manimekalai:16:60-77.reading: Because Saathuvan had learned their language well, the fierce men stop, bow and talk with him and lead him to their chief, whom he finds sitting with his woman like a bear with its mate in a place full of liquor pots, a reek of rotting flesh and white bones drying; bound to him by the shared tongue, the chief asks in the cool of a tree why he came, hears of his sufferings at sea, and orders his people to give the starving man a young woman, strong liquor and meat.
manimekalai:16:60-77.nuance: Saathuvan is saved by learning, not by virtue: knowing the Nagas' speech (பாடை, lines 60 and 70) turns him from food into a guest. The chief's welcome is generous by his own lights, offering what he holds most valuable, which sets up the coming debate as a clash of goods rather than of kindness and cruelty.
manimekalai:16:60-77.event: Saathuvan speaks to the Nagas in their language and is led to their chief, who orders a woman, liquor and meat to be given to him.

manimekalai:16:78-89.reading: Saathuvan, dismayed, says he has heard a cruel word and wants none of it; the chief, provoked to anger, asks what use there is for men in the world without women and food and bids him show it if there is any; Saathuvan answers that the faultless have forbidden deluding liquor and the killing of living beings, because dying and being born are like sleeping and waking, and the doers of good reach a good world and the doers of ill a hard hell.
manimekalai:16:78-89.nuance: The man who lost everything to a courtesan and to dice now refuses a woman and liquor offered as hospitality, so the refusal reads as the reversal of his fall in the first unit. His reason for abstaining is not disgust but a world-view: abstinence follows from rebirth and its fruits. Line 86-87 puts the sleep-and-waking simile of Kural 339 in other words (உறங்கலும் விழித்தலும்), too far from the couplet's wording to count as an echo. The sentence runs on into line 90.
manimekalai:16:78-89.event: Saathuvan refuses the woman, liquor and meat; the angry chief challenges him and Saathuvan explains why the wise forbid liquor and killing.

claims.claim: without women and food there is no gain for men in this world
the faultless have forbidden liquor and the killing of living beings
death and birth follow one another as sleep and waking do
those who do good reach a good world and those who do ill reach hell

manimekalai:16:90-106.reading: Saathuvan ends that the wise gave these things up because they understood this; the chief laughs harshly and demands to be told plainly how a life that runs out of the body takes on a form and enters another place; Saathuvan, without anger, argues that the body feels while life dwells in it, but once life leaves, the body feels nothing though it is cut and burned, so something has gone out of it; that the departed have a dwelling everyone knows, not he alone; that in dreams the life goes many leagues while the body stays here; and that, going so, the life enters the body its own deeds have put on.
manimekalai:16:90-106.nuance: Saathuvan answers a request for a mechanism with two proofs by inference: the corpse's insensibility (lines 96-99) and the dream journey (lines 102-103), each leading to the conclusion that something leaves the body. It is a lay merchant's argument, not a monk's, and it speaks of a life (உயிர்) that travels and enters a new body, which the Buddhist teaching later in the epic would put differently; the text names no school for it. The chief had already granted the soul in his question (line 92 repeats what he was told), so the argument persuades him without his ever conceding the premise in words.
manimekalai:16:90-106.event: The chief mockingly asks how a life can pass into another body, and Saathuvan answers him with the corpse and the dream.

claims.claim: since a body cut and burned after death feels nothing, something that felt has gone out of it
in dreams the life travels far while the body stays, so the life can leave the body
the departing life enters the body that its own deeds have fitted to it

manimekalai:16:107-116.reading: The chief falls at the feet of the merchant who knows the good and says that if he gives up liquor and meat he cannot keep alive the life within this body, so he asks to be told a good dharma that suits them until they die in their own way; Saathuvan praises the request, says he will tell the dharma within his reach, and bids him, if shipwrecked men come here alive, to stop killing and protect their lives, and, leaving aside the beasts that die of old age, to give up harm toward every living thing.
manimekalai:16:107-116.nuance: Saathuvan does not ask the Nagas for the full abstinence he practises; he scales dharma to what they can bear (உன் தனக்கு ஒல்லும் நெறி அறம், line 113). The sense of line 116 is not certain: மூத்து விளி மா ஒழித்து seems to set aside animals that die of age as the one flesh still allowed, flesh that needs no killing, but it may instead belong with the prohibition. The command closes at line 117.
manimekalai:16:107-116.event: The chief, persuaded, asks for a dharma he can keep, and Saathuvan gives him a lesser rule: spare the shipwrecked and harm no living thing.

claims.claim: without liquor and meat the life in this body cannot be kept
dharma may be fitted to what a person can keep: spare the shipwrecked, eat only what dies of age, and harm no living being

manimekalai:16:117-135.reading: The chief promises to keep this dharma and bids Saathuvan take the precious goods fit for him, the fragrant wood, fine cloth and heaps of treasure of men from wrecked ships whom they had eaten before; Saathuvan boards Chandradattan's ship when it comes, returns to this city, lives with Aathirai and gives many gifts from his house; Kayasandigai bids Manimekalai take alms from such an Aathirai's hand, and when Manimekalai enters and stands like an unadorned picture, Aathirai bows, circles her and fills the wide bowl Amudasurabi, saying 'may the disease of hunger be cut off from the whole earth', and gives the food that is medicine for precious life.
manimekalai:16:117-135.nuance: The wealth that ends the story is the plunder of men the Nagas ate, now given as a teacher's fee and spent on charity at home; the cannibal's hoard becomes the merchant's alms. The voice's prophecy is fulfilled in a single line (line 124). Kayasandigai's speech ends at line 129, and lines 130-135 are the poet's narration. Aathirai's wish at line 134 turns one gift into a vow for the whole earth, and line 135 names the food ஆருயிர்மருந்து, a name the bowl's story uses elsewhere.
manimekalai:16:117-135.event: Saathuvan returns home rich on Chandradattan's ship; Aathirai puts the first alms into Manimekalai's bowl.

claims.claim: food given to the hungry is the medicine that saves life

links.note: The voice in the burning ground names the merchant Chandradattan and his ship; at the end of the tale Saathuvan comes home on Chandradattan's ship, as foretold.
links.teaches: The prophecy that stopped Aathirai's death is kept only after Saathuvan has converted his captors, so the voice in effect promised a return that his own learning and argument had still to earn.

links.note: Madhavi listed the ways of the pathini: die at once with a sigh, enter the blazing fire as if it were a cool pool, or wear down the body in vows; Aathirai takes the second way, and the fire will not have her, and she leaves it like a woman coming back from a bath (16:46).
links.teaches: Madhavi's list assumes the fire completes the pathini's choice, but Aathirai's fire refuses her, so the epic shows that a pathini's power can overrule even her own resolve to die and makes Madhavi's simile of the cool pool literally true.

links.note: Saathuvan argues from the insensible corpse and the dream journey that a life leaves the body and enters another fitted by its deeds; the materialist of kaathai 27 holds that awareness ends when the elements part, that inference is no means of knowledge, and that a next world of fruits is a lie.
links.teaches: The materialist's challenge is met eleven kaathais before he states it, by a merchant using exactly the inference the materialist refuses to accept, so the pair shows that the epic's case for rebirth stands or falls on whether inference counts as knowledge.

links.note: Saathuvan tells the Naga chief that the dying of the born and the birth of the dead are like sleeping and waking, the simile of Kural 339 in other words, and draws from it that good deeds lead to a good world and ill to hell.
links.teaches: The couplet's simile is a calm statement of impermanence, but Saathuvan turns it into the premise of an argument against liquor and killing, showing that the image of sleep and waking implies a self that wakes again and must answer for its acts.

gains.a: Saathuvan's premise gains a formulation already familiar as a saying, which is why he can offer it to a sceptic without proof
gains.b: the couplet gains a moral consequence it never draws, that what one does before sleeping decides where one wakes

links.note: Saathuvan is ruined by a courtesan and by dice and cast off penniless; among the Nagas he refuses the woman and liquor offered him, and comes home with treasure.
links.teaches: The couplet names double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those Fortune has left, and the story runs the rule both ways: two of the three strip Saathuvan of wealth, and his refusal of a woman and liquor on the island is what brings fortune back.

gains.a: the tale's two halves gain a single rule that ties his ruin to his later refusal
gains.b: the couplet gains a reversal it does not state, that leaving the three restores what keeping them lost

links.note: The couplet's highest wife commands the rain; here the chaste wives who bring down the rain themselves worship Aathirai, whom fire would not burn.
links.teaches: The epic places a rank above the Kural's summit of wifely power, and grounds it not in daily worship of the husband but in a wife's readiness to die for a husband who had deserted her for a courtesan.

gains.a: Aathirai's praise gains a fixed measure, the rain-bringing wife, against which her rank can be stated
gains.b: the couplet gains the sign that its power is not the highest, and that it can be tested against a husband who did nothing to deserve it

links.note: The Kural argues that no one would sell flesh if no one killed to eat; Saathuvan, told the Nagas cannot live without meat, lets them keep only the flesh of beasts that die of age and bids them harm no living thing.
links.teaches: The couplet treats the eater as the cause of all killing, while Saathuvan finds the one flesh no killing supplies and so gives people who cannot give up meat a way to keep the Kural's end without its whole demand.

gains.a: Saathuvan's concession gains the reasoning that makes it a principle: what is wrong is the killing that eating causes
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where its rule must bend to what a people can bear, and a shape the bending can take

links.note: Saathuvan argues that the departing life enters the body its deeds put on, as a reason for the Nagas to do good; Tirumular bids the reader seek the way by which, leaving this body, one does not enter another.
links.teaches: The same passage of the life into a new body is good news in the epic, a reason to act well for a better world, and the thing to be escaped in Tirumular, so the pair shows that a merchant's ethics of rebirth stops short of the release both traditions put beyond it.

gains.a: Saathuvan's argument gains the reminder that a good rebirth is still a rebirth, which the epic leaves to its later teaching
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a reasoned account, from the corpse and the dream, of the entry into another body that it simply assumes

links.note: The Kural says the evil disease called hunger will not touch one used to sharing his food; Aathirai fills the inexhaustible bowl saying 'may the disease of hunger be cut off from the whole earth'.
links.teaches: The couplet promises that sharing guards the sharer from the disease of hunger, while Aathirai's gift, poured into a bowl that never empties, aims to cure the disease for everyone, so the pair moves from the giver's safety to a cure for the world.

gains.a: Aathirai's phrase பசிப் பிணி gains the couplet's account of hunger as a disease that sharing keeps away
gains.b: the couplet gains an image of sharing that no longer protects one household but is meant to empty hunger from the earth

new_concepts.gloss: the chaste wife whose virtue carries power
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word: பத்தினிப் பெண்டிரும் (50)

source_issues: Line 105: the edition's ௌ before a vowel sign was read as ெள (தௌி repaired to தெளி); the repair fits the sense 'know clearly'.
